patterns.name: “No X, no Y” chains
patterns.description: Two or more “no …” items in a row, e.g. “No fluff, no filler, no jargon.” The badge counts the “no” items.
notes: The Tengo script counts literal "no " and "no-" substrings per line instead of recognising the reference chain grammar and separators.

Separate sentences can produce a false positive, and multiple chains on one line merge into one alert. Word boundaries and flexible whitespace are not preserved. The reference item-count badge is not implemented.

patterns.name: “That’s the whole …”
patterns.description: “That / this is the whole point, game, thing …”
notes: The reference accepts that/this with straight or curly apostrophes, is/was, and an optional arbitrary noun after "the whole".
This rule restricts the noun to point/game/pitch, requires that noun, omits "this's", and does not accept curly apostrophes.

patterns.name: “Did not X, did not Y” chains
patterns.description: Two or more “did not …” or “didn’t …” items in a row. The badge counts the items.
notes: Curly-apostrophe "didn’t" and flexible whitespace are not recognised by the literal substring counter.
The script counts a whole line rather than a contiguous chain, so separate sentences can produce a false positive and multiple chains merge. The reference item count is not reported.

patterns.name: “Don’t VERB it … VERB it”
patterns.description: “Don’t call it X. Call it Y.” — a negated verb + “it”, then the same verb + “it” again.
notes: The script handles only the first two dot-separated segments of a line beginning with straight-apostrophe "don't" or "do not".
Curly apostrophes, just/simply/merely modifiers, em/en dashes, semicolons, colons, other reference separators, and quoted sentence endings are not preserved.
It only compares the repeated verb prefix and never requires "it" on both sides; "Don't open the door. Open a window." is a false positive.

patterns.name: “Sit with that”
patterns.description: The reflective “sit with that / this / it (for a moment)”, plus “sit with the discomfort” and friends.
notes: The reference also matches "sits" and "sitting", either "the" or "your" before every listed feeling, and singular/plural "feeling(s)".
This rule only matches "sit", permits "your" only with plural "feelings", and omits "the feelings". The optional "for a WORD" suffix is not part of its match.

patterns.name: “You already know”
patterns.description: “You already know” — the answer, what to do, or standing alone before a full stop.
notes: The reference permits "you already knows", mid-sentence matches before its recognised complements, and bare "you already know" only when no following word remains.
This rule is sentence-initial (with optional "deep down,") and supports fewer complements. Its optional complement also allows false positives such as sentence-initial "You already know Python".

patterns.name: “Is the entire …”
patterns.description: “X is the entire point / game / business model.”
notes: The is-the-entire reference accepts is/was/are/were and straight/curly contractions followed by an optional arbitrary word. This rule restricts the verb and noun lists.
The the-entire-is reference accepts one to five words before is/was/are/were. This rule only accepts point/business model/exercise/pitch followed directly by is/was.

patterns.name: “The entire … is”
patterns.description: “The entire point / game / business model is …” — the flipped twin of “is the entire”.
notes: The is-the-entire reference accepts is/was/are/were and straight/curly contractions followed by an optional arbitrary word. This rule restricts the verb and noun lists.
The the-entire-is reference accepts one to five words before is/was/are/were. This rule only accepts point/business model/exercise/pitch followed directly by is/was.

patterns.name: “Is real … and / not”
patterns.description: “The X is real, and / not …”, including “is the real … and it”. Skips “real estate”, “real time”, and similar.
notes: The reference accepts arbitrary subjects but requires a later "and" or "not"; the "is the/a real ..." branch additionally requires "it". It excludes real estate/time/life/world/quick.
This rule uses a subject whitelist and a separate "this is the real work" phrase. It misses subjects such as loss and also flags standalone "The improvement is real.", which the reference does not.

patterns.name: “The punchline is”
patterns.description: “The punchline is …”, “the punchline:”, or “the punchline?”.
notes: The reference accepts is/was/being after "the punchline" and accepts a colon or question mark without an intervening space.
This rule only accepts "is" as a verb and requires whitespace before the punctuation alternatives, missing ordinary "The punchline:" and "The punchline?".

patterns.name: “Worth naming”
patterns.description: The therapist-voiced “that loss is real and it’s worth naming”, “it’s worth naming that …”, or a “Worth naming:” opener. Skips “naming names”.
notes: The reference accepts is/are/was/were/feel(s)/felt/seem(s)/seemed or a contraction, zero to two intervening words, and "worth naming:" with optional whitespace before the colon.
This rule restricts the subjects and forms, requires "that" after "it's/it is worth naming", and omits curly apostrophes.
Its trailing word boundary after the colon prevents a normal "Worth naming: ..." match. The general reference exclusion for "naming names" is not reproduced.

patterns.name: “That’s not nothing”
patterns.description: “That is not nothing” / “that’s not nothing”, plus the “this / it / which is not nothing” variants.
notes: The reference accepts that/this/it/which with is/was or straight/curly contractions.
This rule only lists that's/that is/this is/it is/which is. It misses "it's", "this's", "which's", all was forms, and curly apostrophes.

patterns.name: AI vocabulary words
patterns.description: Words LLMs lean on far more than people do: “delve”, “tapestry”, “meticulous”, “pivotal”, “intricate”, “interplay”, “underscore”, “garner”, “bolster”, “vibrant”, “bustling”, “multifaceted”, “seamless”, “ever-evolving”. One hit can be coincidence — several is a tell.
notes: The highlighter includes "intricacies". The current "intricat(?:e|ely|acies)" alternative instead accepts the misspelling "intricatacies" and misses "intricacies". Other vocabulary alternatives are represented.

patterns.name: “Not just X, but Y”
patterns.description: Negative parallelisms: “not just X, but (also) Y”, “not only … but …”, and the “it’s not X — it’s Y” contrast.
notes: The reference accepts curly contractions and was forms, with comma, en/em dash, or semicolon contrast separators. This rule omits curly contractions, was forms, commas, and en dashes.

The reference first branch stops at sentence punctuation, newline, or semicolon. The current first branch has a 120-character limit and can span sentence punctuation; the second branch uses an 80-character limit rather than the reference 60.

patterns.name: “It’s important to note”
patterns.description: Didactic hedging: “it is important to note that”, “it’s worth noting”, “it should be noted”.
notes: The reference accepts straight/curly contractions, is/was, optional "also", and noting/mentioning/remembering forms.
The current whitespace before the contraction alternative prevents normal "it's/it’s" from matching. Was forms, "also", "worth mentioning", and "worth remembering" are also absent.

patterns.name: “Stands as a testament”
patterns.description: “Stands / serves as a testament (or reminder)”, “is a testament to” — inflating significance instead of saying what happened.
notes: The reference includes stand/stands/stood/standing and serve/serves/served/serving, a/an, and an optional modifier before testament/reminder.
This rule only uses stands/serves with "a" and no modifier. Its other branch omits was/are/were/remain and modifiers before "testament to".

patterns.name: “Plays a crucial role”
patterns.description: “Plays a crucial / pivotal / vital / key / significant role in …”.
notes: The reference accepts a/an and an optional modifier before crucial/pivotal/vital/key/significant/central/critical/important.
This rule requires "a" directly before the adjective, missing "an important role" and "a truly pivotal role".

patterns.name: “Ever-evolving landscape”
patterns.description: Scene-setting boilerplate: “the ever-evolving / changing / shifting landscape”, “in today’s fast-paced world”.
notes: The reference accepts ever-evolving/ever-changing/ever-shifting landscape and any following word in its "in today's/today’s ..." branch.
This rule omits ever-changing/ever-shifting and curly apostrophes, and requires the final word "world" instead of accepting economy/industry or another word.

patterns.name: “Experts argue”
patterns.description: Vague attribution to unnamed authorities: “experts argue”, “some critics have noted”, “observers suggest”, “industry reports indicate”.
notes: The reference combines every listed authority with a broad verb set, optional many/some/several/most/numerous, optional have/often/widely, and past-tense variants.

This rule has separate, narrower subject/verb combinations and omits agree/contend/observe/caution/cite plus many tense/adverb variants. It also requires plural "industry reports" and omits inflected report verbs.

patterns.name: “Despite these challenges”
patterns.description: The boilerplate challenges-and-outlook formula: “despite these challenges”, “faces several challenges”, “challenges remain”, “remains to be seen”.
notes: The reference permits these/those/such/its/their/the/numerous/significant/ongoing plus an optional word before "challenges".
This rule only includes these/such/significant with no intervening word and only "faces", missing face/faced/facing. The "challenges remain" and "remains to be seen" alternatives are represented.

patterns.name: Participle sentence tails
patterns.description: Superficial analysis bolted onto a sentence end: “…, highlighting / underscoring / showcasing / reflecting the …”.
notes: The reference detector and this rule recognise the same comma, participle, and following-word alternatives.
Match-span difference: the reference highlights the rest of the clause up to sentence punctuation or newline; this rule matches only the opening phrase.

patterns.name: Promotional boilerplate
patterns.description: Travel-brochure tone: “nestled in”, “in the heart of”, “rich tapestry / heritage”, “hidden gem”, “boasts a”, “breathtaking”, “stunning views”.
notes: The reference also matches "nestled at", singular "boast", and "rich cultural/historical history/tapestry". These alternatives are missing here.
The remaining listed promotional alternatives are represented. Legacy LegPromotional.Language catches some phrases but does not supply complete coverage of this pattern.

patterns.name: Chatbot leftovers
patterns.description: Artifacts pasted straight from a chatbot: “as an AI language model”, “as of my last update”, “knowledge cutoff”, plus markup debris like “oaicite”, “contentReference”, “turn0search” and “utm_source=” tracking parameters.
notes: The reference combines cannot/can't/do not/don't (straight or curly) with either browse the internet or access real-time/realtime. This rule implements only a subset and requires the hyphen in real-time.

The reference accepts turn0search/news/image without a trailing digit and metadata substrings inside larger tokens. This rule requires a trailing digit and adds word boundaries, while broadening the turn number beyond zero.
